134.t: Popular styles of the day: Waller, Armstrong, Ellington, Henderson
134.s: He says Waller and Armstrong set the style, Ellington was over most heads, and discusses Henderson's and Redman's arranging.
134.ch: Chicago repertoire, bands and the end of the big-band era
134.q: To me, two men set the style of the day. It was – of the jazz during that period. It was Fats Waller and Louis Armstrong. Now the Duke’s music was always great, but it was over most folks’ heads, because he’s using this minor ninths thing way back. But everybody knew his music was great, and…

134.t: The recording ban, singers and the stars of Lunceford's band
134.s: He says singers rose in the ban and names Lunceford's Joe Thomas, Willie Smith and Freddie Webster.
134.q: Yeah. When you couldn’t record? That caused a lot of stuff to go down. That when singers came to the fore, because back when I was a kid, we’d go see the big bands. They’d always have some singers that would sit on the side. They might sing two numbers a night. One. Nobody cared, because we’re all…

90.t: The Gay Floyd band from Little Rock
90.s: He praises an overlooked Arkansas band with a five-man reed section, a sleeper bus, writer Riley Hampton and entertainer Cleophus Jackson.
90.ch: Touring shows and the bands he heard
90.q: Oh, a band that really impressed me, and nobody never, ever mentions this band... A band that came from Little Rock, Arkansas -- Gay(?) Floyd. They had a fantastic band. They had a five-man reed section. They had the two tenors, alto and the baritone. They had full brass, a full band. They had a…

90.t: Jukebox records and the Erskine Hawkins band
90.s: Ice cream parlor jukeboxes with Erskine Hawkins, Roy Eldridge and Krupa, and a rundown of Hawkins's sidemen.
90.ch: Touring shows and the bands he heard
90.q: There were so many, so many great things, you know. Then the jukeboxes were popular in the ice cream parlors. You know, you'd go by, take your girlfriend to buy some ice cream sodas and stuff, or milkshakes, and you'd play the jukebox. You know, I used to listen to the great records by Erskine…

70.t: Hearing Fletcher Henderson's band in Cincinnati in 1930
70.s: Jackson calls it the most fantastic band he had heard and lists its trumpets, trombones, saxophones and rhythm section with Kirby, Walter Johnson and Clarence Holiday.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: I remember way back when -- well, the first time I heard that band that I thought it was the most fantastic band I had ever heard and that was in 1930. I heard them in Cincinnati, Ohio.

70.t: Russell Procope and the John Kirby sextet
70.s: Procope read anything; the Kirby band, he says, was the greatest little band, swinging classics sensibly in the best hotels.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: play the music that band played. It had a lot of class. They had a lot of rhythm, and it was a cleancut little band, and they always played the best of jobs, always played hotels and things because they would take classics and turn them into swing, but they would do it sensibly.

147.t: John Kirby's group and McKinney's Cotton Pickers
147.s: Crawford discusses John Kirby's small band showing Lunceford's influence and wonders how McKinney's Cotton Pickers gathered such musicians.
147.q: Band in the land." Yes, that band -- and McKinney's Cotton Pickers, back in Detroit. Now, how did he assemble all those great musicians in his band? Fathead on alto, even got Don Redman in there. We used to call him the Little Giant. Yeah, Little Giant. And he had -- and I don't know what…

147.t: Speed Webb's band and McKinney's Cotton Pickers
147.s: Crawford praises Speed Webb's swinging band with Roy Eldridge and wonders how McKinney's Cotton Pickers got Don Redman and Cuba Austin.
147.ch: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
147.q: Yes, I don't care what nobody say. I don't think -- well, other drummers and musicians have gone through the same things, you know, I imagine, but I didn't meet a lot of guys until I finally hit New York. There was a band, one of the swingingest bands I've

770.s: Names Harry James, Ray McKinley, Jimmy Joy and others from Texas; Alfonso Trent and Boots and His Buddies mentioned.
770.q: Yes, we did. Harry James is from Texas, and Ray McKinley is from Texas, and, uh, Jimmy Joy, of course. Jimmy Maloney played wonderful clarinet. He's from Texas. It turned out some very good boys over there. Oh, we sure did.

431.t: Pre-swing big bands and saxophonists admired
431.s: Pre-swing bands groping toward swing; Pat Davis and Hutchinrider are recalled.
431.q: Yeah, I don't think I would like him today, but he played in the Eysom Jones band. These are all pre-swing bands, but there were a lot of bands that played big band jazz. That didn't come out with the swing era, nor you know it's often said that that problem was solved with Fletcher Henderson when…

908.t: Big touring bands of the 1930s: McKinney's, Henderson, Ellington
908.s: He recalls the big road bands of the 30s, naming McKinney's Cotton Pickers, Fletcher Henderson, Duke Ellington, Alphonso Trent and Noble Sissle, and Goldkette's booking.
908.q: Well the two biggest bands that I remember, or not the two bands, I had a whole lot of bands that traveled but they were big bands you see. But we had regular work. But these other jobs they had one-nighters like Fletcher Henderson, McKinney's Cotton Pickers. They were the first bands that I can…

22.t: Article continued: early recording bands and imitators of the ODJB
22.s: The reading lists early recording bands and Clarence Williams's Blue Five; La Rocca says Fletcher Henderson copied the Dixieland Jazz Band records.
22.ch: Clarence Williams's 1936 article and the dispute
22.q: They were imitators of the Dixieland Jazz Band. Fletcher Henderson was one of the first colored men to copy from the records of the Dixieland Jazz Band.

706.t: Listening to elders; Fletcher Henderson band and the Lanin and Lopez bands
706.s: Armstrong says he preferred the elders as a teenager, lists Fletcher Henderson band members at the Roseland at 24, and tells of hearing Sam Lanin's and Vincent Lopez's bands and an older trumpeter, B. A. Rolfe, playing seriously.
706.q: but it's in him yeah and but the average kid would say I don't want to play that I want to play uh uh uh uh I'm with you on that you know when I was a teenager I listened to the good old greats you know what I mean the boys around my crowd was gonna go to the next neighborhood and fight and all…

820.t: Listening to Fletcher Henderson and Goldkette bands
820.s: The Owls listened to Henderson and Jean Goldkette records; Netto recalls the steady swing feel on second and fourth beats.
820.q: Yeah, we listened to Fletcher Henderson and that other band from Canada up there. What was the name of that? You know? Canada? I think they were, well, I don't know if they were Canadians, but they were playing up in Canada. Radio came in around 20- Is this a black group? No, I don't believe. I…

311.t: Favorite bands: Jimmie Lunceford and Duke Ellington's Lawrence Brown
311.s: Lunceford was his model; he played Ellington tunes and was friends with trombonist Lawrence Brown, whose father preached in San Francisco.
311.q: Well my favorite band, my first favorite band of all time in the beginning was Jimmie Lunceford. Jimmie Lunceford knocked me out. That’s what I tried to pattern my style after. “Sweet Swing.”

537.t: Louis Armstrong's influence on jazz, Henderson band and brass playing
537.s: Brunious and Barrett discuss Armstrong's transformation of the Henderson band, the Swing Era, and his effect on brass vibrato; Brunious criticizes a professor who belittled him.
537.q: I was sitting there in admiration of your comments, especially about Louis Armstrong, who, without him, I really don’t know what position jazz would be — I don’t know if there would even be jazz actually.

155.t: Favorite bands of the 1930s, lyrics, and meeting Johnny Mercer and Condon's band
155.s: Coon-Sanders and McKinney's Cotton Pickers, his love of lyrics, and the postwar Condon's lineup.
155.q: I knew more favorites than individuals. I suppose that Coon Sanders, I loved to hear them play. McKinney’s Cotton Pickers was a jazz band. There’s a new one now in Detroit but this was the old one. I just knew the name, I never saw them. “It’s Tight Like That” was a © Hamilton College Jazz Archive…

165.t: Ellington's wish to match Fletcher Henderson; Lunceford's show band
165.s: Duke Ellington wanted only to approach Henderson's band; Hendricks recalls Lunceford's costume changes in Toledo.
165.q: I was surprised when he told me that all he wanted to have was an orchestra that would approach Fletcher Henderson’s. I said whoa.

422.t: Blindfold test: Lunceford's 'Rhythm Is Our Business'
422.s: He identifies Lunceford, praises its cleanness and the recorded bass, contrasting Ellington and Lunceford with Henderson.
422.q: Oh yeah, um, I don’t know what take, but it’s Jimmie Lunceford Orchestra, “Rhythm is our Business.” But there are two takes. I can’t tell you which one.

611.t: Lunceford against Basie, and Fletcher Henderson as king of swing
611.s: He never worked with Basie but rates Lunceford's band as better entertainment, and recalls three years with Henderson, who pioneered swing and added Hawkins, Carter and Armstrong.
611.q: No I haven’t. No I haven’t. I wish I did. But I tell you I did work with a band that, well I may be saying something that people will agree, you know, but I had a pleasure working with Jimmie Lunceford and I thought it was a greater band than Count Basie. Not musically. Not musically. Exclusive…

62.t: Arrangers of the swing bands and Duke as idol
62.s: Lunceford's arrangers and the era's great arrangers (Fletcher Henderson, Edgar Sampson, others) are named; Wilson calls Ellington his idol.
62.ch: Lunceford, Ellington, Gillespie and the big bands
62.q: Well, um. As I said – first of all, Jimmie um he – he had lots of arrangers he didn’t just have – first he had Sy Oliver. What he did was – he had the man who was taking over that year as the top arranger in the world of jazz. That’s – that’s now, what’s his name? Fletcher Henderson was of course…

371.t: A couple of months with John Kirby's band
371.s: Jones briefly played in Kirby's small band, praising Charlie Shavers's writing and the band's big sound.
371.q: Interesting, because he had Bill Beason, Buster Bailey. That took Billy Cobham’s place for a while. I was overtime. I played with the band sure maybe a couple of months. But Charlie Shavers used to do a lot of the writing for the band. Of course, you know Charlie, he kept playing higher, and…

108.t: So many bands, and players moving between them
108.s: He recalls the abundance of bands and constant personnel movement.
108.ch: The swing era and jazz history
108.q: True. Yeah. There was a great deal of it. Some musicians would like one band better than they liked another, and they would do whatever they could to become members of that band.

80.t: First hearing Charlie Johnson's loud brass section in Philadelphia
80.s: He first met the band at a Philadelphia dance, with Ham Davis and Rex Stewart in the loudest brass he ever heard, and mentions who arranged for them.
80.ch: New York, Henderson and Charlie Johnson
80.q: the money, you can't draw the people out, I don't know, what you going to do? Now they came to Philadelphia. That's where I first met him. He was playing a dance date there, and I met him and the band, and they had a hell of a band. And they were blowing the walls down.

230.t: Personnel of the Paramount band and Hammond's Melody Maker praise
230.s: Barnet names the sidemen, led by arranger Nathan Van Cleve, and recalls Hammond's review of the special arrangements and the musicians' ball.
230.ch: Harlem, 52nd Street and the first big bands
230.q: Yeah. Well, the guy that was making all the arrangements was Nathan Van Cleve, who later became quite a big heavy in the studios here, out in the West Coast, arranging. He was playing trumpet in the band. Johnny Dillard, Bob Kuzamano, and Doug Shoffner. That was the trumpet section. And the…

9.t: Fletcher Henderson's band with Armstrong in Boston, 1925
9.s: He heard Henderson's precise band with Armstrong, Hawkins, Redman and Buster Bailey, and names its personnel.
9.ch: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
9.q: : Yeah. Louis was really blowin' something like I never heard before. But I didn't appreciate him, because he didn't look nice. But I didn't know... I shouldn't put this in there.

106.s: Briggs found the Henderson arrangements and tenor tone rough and wanted more refinement for patrons, though he admired Buster Bailey.
106.q: And I'd say Fletcher Anderson, his arrangements were good, but to my liking, I think they were a little -- that's the way I feel.

28.t: Duke or Fletcher: the best big band of 1928-33
28.s: Asked which band was the best, Butler says it was a toss-up between Ellington and Henderson, with Chick Webb also fine.
28.ch: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
28.q: Well, it was a toss-up between Duke and Fletcher. You see, Fletcher had a stomp band, see, Fletcher and they would battle had a stomp band and Fletcher would come up there/every year, you know. Chick Webb had a beautiful band but Fletcher and Duke, they was the kings. They was the kings.

382.s: Campbell recites the Kirby sextet's personnel and handles a Columbia record of 'Loch Lomond'.
382.q: I bet he doesn't have that "Flow Gently, Sweet Rhythm" there.

758.s: Speed Webb's band was as good as Lunceford's but never reached New York.
758.q: : So then I went with Speed Webb. That was a good band. A very good band. I just wish that band could have got to New York, to ...(?)...(?)... I think that band would have still been going today. That band was as good as Lunceford's or any of those bands, really.

91.t: Why everyone wanted to play with Henderson
91.s: The Henderson band was THE band to musicians of the day, with Smith, Hawkins, Redman and Bailey.
91.ch: Fletcher Henderson and forming his own band
91.q: You know, we all used to listen to Henderson records, and you know, it sounded all very exciting. Joe Smith, that wonderful trumpet player, and Coleman Hawkins and Don Redman and Buster Bailey on the clarinet. Oh, we just loved this band, you know. Everybody wanted to play with Fletcher Henderson.

234.t: The style of his first band and its influences
234.s: Gil says ensemble playing was his style. He lists Ellington, Don Redman, McKinney's Cotton Pickers, Red Nichols and Casa Loma.
234.ch: Japan trip, publishing and early influences
234.q: Ensemble I guess was really the style ................(VOICE FADES OUT). That would be things for everybody to play, you know, ensemble. Not just an ordinary ensemble but something with some (sincerity and spirit?) that we could all do together.

18.s: He names Fletcher Henderson, John Kirby's group and McKinney's Cotton Pickers.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: I don't know if I was in the band then or not, but I know he had the band.

99.t: Hearing Fletcher Henderson at the Chicago Armory
99.s: He names every member of Henderson's band, from Hawkins and Buster Bailey to Tommy Ladnier, and meets them during the week Tunney beat Dempsey.
99.q: And we got to Chicago. And the Chicago Defender, they gave us free tickets to go to that affair. And Doc, I was the happiest person in the world, because I had all my life -- see, Fletcher Henderson's band was the hottest band out at that time, see. His band had been hot from the early 20's on up…

386.t: Alphonso Trent's band, rated A, and why it bypassed New York
386.s: He praises Trent's early band and Morgenstern relays why they avoided the Arcadia in New York.
386.q: It's a funny thing, though, Dan, that a band like Alphonso Trent whom I give an A' rating... and I guess I was influenced by the fact that it was the first, you know, organized from band that I heard. Because Trent started/like a five-piece band to go on to become, you know, a twelve-or…

388.t: The Kirby sextet's quality and the Barnet battle at the 1939 World's Fair
388.s: Leeman praises the band's impeccable musicians and Shavers's difficult book, recalling the Kirby group nearly outswinging Barnet's 16 pieces with O'Neil Spencer on drums.
388.ch: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
388.q: Before me, the band was comprised of impeccable musicians, Buster Bailey's thoroughly -- because Charlie Shavers wrote a book that was pretty rough to play, and they played impeccably. Every member. By the same token, Billy Kyle fed that band, and I played against them with Charlie Barnet, doing…

236.t: Lunceford's band at Casa Manana and Eddie Wilcox's arrangements
236.s: Rowles thinks the Lunceford band outplayed everyone and credits Eddie Wilcox with many arrangements.
236.q: take Duke Ellington, you take the whole works, put them all together, and Jimmie Lunceford would blow them out of the place.

115.t: Preferring Ellington and Horace Henderson to Fletcher Henderson
115.s: He liked Ellington better than Fletcher Henderson and Horace Henderson's swing better still, disliking Fletcher's piano.
115.q: But as far as his musicians and everything, he had good musicians. Fletch had good musicians. But I just didn't care much for his piano playing. That was the only thing.

31.t: Black bands of the 1920s: Fletcher Henderson, Sam Wooding, Charlie Johnson
31.s: They discuss Fletcher Henderson's Boston waltzes in 1919, Sam Wooding's European band, Charlie Johnson at Small's and Vincent Lopez.
31.ch: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
31.q: No, I don't. Well, I tell you, in 1919 Fletcher Henderson came to Boston and he was the greatest band in the world there, because he could play waltzes, and that's the Massachusetts -- what's the name of the hall up there. Horicultural Hall was crowded, people would come there to hear Fletcher…

75.t: First visit to the Savoy and hearing Rex with Fletcher Henderson
75.s: The Brown Brothers took him to the Savoy where he heard Fletcher Henderson's band with Coleman Hawkins, Walter Johnson and Rex Stewart.
75.ch: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
75.q: I mean, he was a different person than I thought he would be. The first time I saw him playing with Fletcher Henderson... The first time I went to the Savoy,

171.s: Ramey heard Henderson only once or twice and was biased toward Kansas City bands.
171.ch: Parker, Buster Smith and the Kansas City style
171.q: I only heard him once, and that's right after they made that first after they introduced that great [Israel] little bass player, Crosby, they made "Christopher Columbus."
